documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in tourism service work, employees increasingly need to interpret machine-generated outputs, evaluate their usefulness, and integrate them into organisational activities. Yet little is known about the firm-level resource configurations in which workforce human–machine collaborative literacy (HC) accompanies favourable digital transformation performance. Integrating organisational psychology perspectives on human–AI work with the technology–organisation–environment framework and a digital eco-embedding perspective, this study applied fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to 401 managerial questionnaires aggregated to 30 Chinese tourism small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The analysis examined manager-perceived workforce HC alongside intelligent technology infrastructure (TI), digital niche (IO), policy support (PS), and open innovation networks (CN). No individual condition or its negation was necessary for high perceived performance (HC necessity consistency = 0.845). Two high-performance configurations shared core TI and IO: H1 included peripheral CN, with HC unspecified, whereas H2 included peripheral HC and PS. Seven firms satisfied the descriptive membership criterion for both high-performance configurations. Three non-high-performance configurations shared the absence of digital niche (~IO), with the absence of HC specified in two. The intermediate expressions were retained across the examined calibration and truth-table threshold settings. In the leave-one-firm-out analyses, the complete high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 28 of 30 deletions and the H2 conjunction in all 30, whereas the complete non-high-performance intermediate solution was retained in 20 of 30 deletions. These findings position manager-perceived workforce HC as a configuration-specific complement rather than a universally necessary condition for favourable perceived transformation performance. By situating a workforce-related capability within technological, ecosystem, and institutional resource configurations, the study provides an organisational-level contextual perspective on human–AI collaboration. The findings suggest that workforce capability development should be considered alongside technological readiness, digital ecosystem access, and institutional support.

documents.abstract: O artigo examina a escuta praticada pelo líder como fundamento da gestão de pessoas e fonte de vantagem competitiva. A literatura de liderança privilegiou a dimensão emissora da comunicação, ao passo que a escuta permanece pouco investigada como comportamento gerencial. O objetivo consiste em analisar a relação entre a escuta percebida do líder e a segurança psicológica, o comportamento de voz e o engajamento dos membros de equipes de trabalho, considerando o papel moderador da integridade comportamental do líder. Propõe-se um delineamento misto sequencial explanatório, que combina um levantamento com escalas validadas, analisado por modelagem de equações estruturais por mínimos quadrados parciais, e entrevistas semiestruturadas com líderes, tratadas por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados esperados indicam que a escuta se associa positivamente à segurança psicológica, que medeia parcialmente seus efeitos sobre a voz e o engajamento, e que essa relação se intensifica quando há coerência entre o discurso e a prática do líder. Conclui-se que a escuta opera como mecanismo relacional cuja eficácia depende da integridade percebida e que as proposições prescritivas sobre conflito e reconhecimento requerem formulação condicional.

Model Bahasa Besar (LLM) semakin digunakan untuk mendapatkan penerangan dan ringkasan berkaitan Islam, namun kelancaran respons tidak menjamin kesahihan sumber atau kewajaran tafsiran. Masalah ini menimbulkan persoalan tentang bagaimana pengguna menilai kandungan Islam janaan AI sebelum mempercayai atau menyebarkannya. Kajian ini bertujuan membangunkan kerangka konseptual yang menghubungkan pengalaman interaksi reflektif dengan LLM, kompetensi komunikasi digital dan kesedaran etika komunikasi Islam dengan penilaian kritikal serta kepercayaan terkalibrasi. Artikel konseptual ini menggunakan sintesis literatur terarah melalui carian ilmiah terpilih, semakan kebolehkesanan sumber dan pemetaan analitik-konseptual terhadap literatur kepercayaan terhadap automasi, kredibiliti maklumat, literasi AI, autoriti ilmu dan etika komunikasi Islam. Hasil sintesis membentuk lima konstruk dan lima proposisi, dengan penilaian kritikal dicadangkan sebagai pengantara separa antara tiga dimensi awal dan kepercayaan terkalibrasi. Kerangka ini membezakan keyakinan umum terhadap teknologi daripada kesepadanan keyakinan dengan kualiti bukti bagi sesuatu jawapan. Sumbangan kajian terletak pada pengintegrasian kemampuan epistemik dan tanggungjawab etika dalam satu proses penilaian kandungan Islam, serta penyediaan asas yang boleh diuji melalui eksperimen vignette dan ukuran tingkah laku semakan. Implikasi meliputi pendidikan literasi, ketelusan sumber dan penglibatan pihak berkelayakan dalam semakan kandungan.

documents.abstract: Introduction This study aims to update, synthesize, and provide meta-analytical evidence of the associations between specific Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) dimensions and psychological outcomes (burnout and professional efficacy) among physical education (PE) teachers. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, the authors conducted a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis. In May 2026, five major electronic databases, such as Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, PubMed, and EBSCOhost, were searched for peer-reviewed cross-sectional studies examining JD-R antecedent variables and specified psychological outcomes in PE teachers. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria, with a combined sample of 4,341 participants and 77 effect sizes included in the four target pathways. Results Multilevel meta-analyses indicated a positive association between job demands and burnout ( k = 17, r = 0.477, 95% CI [0.376, 0.568], p < 0.001) and a negative association between resources and burnout ( k = 53, r = -0.342, 95% CI [−0.435, −0.241], p < 0.001). Exploratory resource-subgroup estimates were r = −0.350 for personal resources ( k = 30, 95% CI [−0.523, −0.148], p = 0.002), r = −0.291 for organizational and social resources ( k = 7, 95% CI [−0.541, 0.006], p = 0.053), and r = −0.343 for other work-related correlates ( k = 16, 95% CI [−0.401, −0.282], p < 0.001). Exploratory country analyses indicated between-country differences, F (6, 46) = 4.476, p =0.0012. Neither resources nor demands were significantly associated with professional efficacy ( k = 4, r = 0.246, p = 0.517; k = 3, r = −0.432, p = 0.111, respectively). Sensitivity checks confirm the results held. Discussion The magnitude and direction of the link between teaching environments and psychological outcomes depend on specific JD-R dimensions and local cultural contexts. These findings support associations of greater resources with lower burnout and greater demands with higher burnout. Resource-subgroup and country-level findings require cautious interpretation because of the limited number of independent studies. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420261385085 , CRD420261385085.

Online identity typically has been conceptualized either in terms of online social roles or in terms of identification with specific online groups. In this paper we explore whether people can form a meaningful identity from the online domain itself , seeing themselves collectively as ‘online people’, ‘offline people’, or in terms of a hybrid online/offline self-categorization. Results from a survey study of 200 participants supported this idea, such that the means of online, offline, or hybrid person variables were significantly above the midpoint of the scale and the majority of participants identified most strongly in terms of one of these identities. Factor analysis, correlations, variable network analysis, and textual analysis suggested that online and offline social identity are orthogonal constructs. Moreover, online identity was related to, but distinct from, hybrid identity (being a person who lives both online and offline). Supporting predictions derived from social digital identity theory (SDIT), each kind of domain-based identification uniquely predicted higher trust in the relevant ingroup only. Moreover, in line with predictions, online identification uniquely predicted more positive attitudes towards technology. However, contrary to predictions, the different kinds of domain-based social identification did not uniquely predict wellbeing or social cohesion. Hybrid and offline identification also failed to uniquely predict technology attitudes. Furthermore, when controlling for hybrid identification, being more ‘online’ in terms of online technology use did not significantly predict wellbeing or social cohesion outcomes. These findings represent an initial exploration of ‘domain-based’ social identities and their implications.

Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

Access to artificial intelligence does not establish how widely it is used, how it is integrated into workflows, or whether its use persists as an organizational practice. This conceptual article specifies organizational artificial intelligence use in service-sector small and medium-sized enterprises in terms of breadth, depth and routinization. It combines theory synthesis with model development, drawing on a targeted narrative review of technology acceptance, organizational adoption and post-adoption research. The technology–organization–environment and diffusion-of-innovations perspectives organize eight antecedents. The proposed contribution consists of a provisional specification of organizational use, illustrative indicators, coding safeguards and a formative higher-order specification. Three proposition groups, comprising five labeled statements, link selected antecedents to use dimensions and relate organizational use to process innovation and separately assessed operational and financial outcomes. The framework provides a research agenda for measurement development and evaluation, as well as practical questions to consider when measuring deployment, integration and continuity. It does not offer any empirical validation or causal relationships. The framework applies to service firms with 5–200 employees.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly become integrated into educational settings worldwide, prompting governments to develop regulatory responses ranging from guided pedagogical integration to outright restrictions. In March 2026, Indonesia introduced a comprehensive national policy in this domain through a Joint Ministerial Decree signed by seven ministries, which restricted primary and secondary school students from using generative AI tools for schoolwork while requiring AI-use disclosure statements in higher education research. This study critically examined how the decree constructed AI as a source of educational risk and an object of governance and how these representations compared with international normative frameworks that favored guided pedagogical integration over prohibition. Employing critical discourse analysis (CDA), the study examined the decree's provisions, its underlying legal instruments, and public statements issued by the signatory ministers to identify four dominant discursive framings: protectionist, pedagogical, religious-moral, and administrative. The findings indicated that the decree was primarily grounded in a child-protection and risk-avoidance discourse, drawing partly on a preprint study concerning potential cognitive effects that had not yet been independently replicated, rather than consistently reflecting the evidence-based pedagogical approaches advocated in international guidance. The analysis also identified a distinctive Indonesian religious-moral framing of AI-related risks, rooted in national religious education legislation, that lacked a direct counterpart in comparable international policy frameworks. These findings contributed to the emerging literature on AI governance in educational systems across the Global South and highlighted the importance of developing evidence-informed, developmentally appropriate, and context-sensitive policies that balance student protection with responsible pedagogical integration of generative AI.

All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

Active learning has become central to anatomical sciences education, yet its effectiveness largely depends on student engagement. Here we define the anatomical sciences as gross anatomy, surface anatomy, neuroanatomy, embryology, histology, and integrated radiology. Educators dedicate substantial effort to implement flipped classrooms, team-based learning, small-group discussions, and other active learning modalities. Despite these efforts, disengagement persists, with students arriving unprepared, participating minimally, and/or perceiving activities as unrelated to assessment. An engagement-centered perspective clarifies these discrepancies and informs more intentional course design. Here, we examine engagement throughout the entire learning cycle, drawing on self-determination theory, cognitive load perspectives, constructivist and social constructivist views, experiential and transformative learning theories, and constructive alignment theory. Common barriers to pre-class engagement include excessive workload, weak alignment with in-class activities, and low perceived relevance. Suggested responses include concise, goal-directed tasks that are clearly linked to learning objectives and incorporate low-stakes accountability and retrieval practice. During class, psychological safety, calibrated challenge, and structured peer interaction are highlighted as central conditions for participation. After class, brief self-testing, spaced follow-up questions, and structured reflection activities consolidate learning. Assessment is positioned as a primary driver of engagement, with an emphasis on constructive alignment to ensure that objectives, active sessions, and summative tasks all rehearse the same kinds of cognitive work. Overall, effective active learning in the anatomical sciences relies less on instructional format and more on fostering learner engagement.

Purpose Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), this study examines how data richness, as an organisational resource, is associated with business value through two deployment processes, automation and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmentation, and whether they differ in their capacity to generate value. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 366 Greek firms across four sectors were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped mediation analysis and coefficient-difference tests; business value is measured as perceived value from digital technology. Findings Data richness is positively associated with both deployment processes. Automation is positively associated with business value and channels part of the association between data richness and value, whereas AI-enabled augmentation, the less developed process, shows no significant direct association; the difference is statistically significant, revealing an AI augmentation gap. Data richness also retains a significant direct association with value, and additional analyses suggest that the capability associations with value run through enacted digital transformation. Practical implications Firms should build a strategically governed data foundation, expand automation for near-term returns and develop augmentation as a longer-term capability built on skills, role redesign, validation and trust in AI-supported decisions; EuroMed policy instruments can be aligned with this sequencing. Originality/value Drawing on the RBV, the study shows that deployment processes of the same digital resource differ significantly in their association with value, a heterogeneity interpreted as reflecting the maturity of the complementary capabilities each requires, and provides evidence from a resource-constrained Mediterranean economy.

Workplace flexibility has become an important feature of contemporary employment, influencing how employees organize work and manage professional responsibilities. However, flexibility does not automatically produce stronger commitment or improved performance. This conceptual paper examines how workplace flexibility may shape employee commitment and performance through perceived autonomy, work-life balance, and job satisfaction. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory, Self-Determination Theory, the Job Demands-Resources Model, and Conservation of Resources Theory, it develops an integrated framework identifying organizational support and managerial trust as important contextual conditions. Seven propositions explain the anticipated relationships among flexibility, employee attitudes, and performance outcomes. The framework contributes to employee engagement literature by clarifying potential mechanisms and boundary conditions while offering directions for future empirical investigation.

Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

Most organisations generate travel and transport and thus influence traffic safety. Nevertheless, their roles and responsibilities for occupational road safety remain poorly understood. This study examines organisational readiness for occupational road safety with a particular focus on the relationship between organisations’ perceptions of traffic safety and the implementation of traffic safety measures. The study is based on a survey of organisational representatives in 109 companies in Sweden in 2025. The survey consists of two questionnaires capturing organisational commitment and reported measures to improve traffic safety in organisations’ roles as employers and transport buyers. An employer questionnaire focuses on traffic safety requirements for employees’ work-related travel and organisational vehicle fleets, while a transport procurement questionnaire captures the requirements on transport procurement. Organisational readiness for occupational road safety is analysed using Organisational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC), including perceived capacity to influence traffic safety, views on responsibility, and the integration of traffic safety into occupational health and safety (OHS) or sustainability practices. The results show that many organisations have policies for work-related travel and set traffic safety requirements for their vehicles, while such requirements in transport procurement remain limited. Regression analyses indicate that organisations with higher readiness are more likely to set traffic safety requirements, particularly regarding work-related travel. The findings highlight the need to strengthen organisations’ awareness of their roles and responsibilities, clarify expectations for organisations from authorities, and further integrate traffic safety into organisational management systems to reduce road traffic fatalities and injuries, in line with the global road safety agenda, often framed as “saving lives beyond 2025”.

documents.abstract: Debates around generative artificial intelligence frequently organise workplace change through automation and augmentation, leaving less visible the organisational work through which human contribution remains interpretable once production is shared with generative systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 women in business-related apprenticeships in England, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and abductive engagement with sociotechnical AI research, labour-process scholarship and feminist accounts of recognition, the study develops a mechanism-oriented account in which organisational rules delimit legitimate AI use, selected execution tasks accelerate, and verification, contextual judgement and accountable decision-making remain attached to apprentices. Where AI-mediated production made polished output a weaker standalone indicator of individual capability, some participants described supplementing performance with additional evidentiary work that rendered contribution, judgement and responsibility more legible to evaluators. This evaluator-facing work is conceptualised as attributional labour, a reconfiguration of pre-existing recognition demands whose form changes when technologically mediated artefacts reveal less about the human competence behind them. The organisational costs and returns associated with this work appeared to vary with occupational hierarchy, managerial proximity and the valuation of administrative and relational work. Augmentation consequently emerges as an organisational recognition settlement in which technical capacity, hidden human work and evaluative authority are redistributed together.

Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study examines how workload relates to innovative behavior through emotional exhaustion. Prior research offers competing predictions regarding the consequences of workload, particularly from the JD–R model and the challenge–hindrance stressor perspective. Against this backdrop, we propose that workload is negatively related to innovative behavior through its positive association with emotional exhaustion. We further examine how two key job resources—empowering leadership and perceived organizational support (POS)—jointly shape this process. Using three‐wave, multisource data from 349 employees nested within 30 supervisors in a large Chinese firm, we find that workload is negatively associated with innovative behavior and that this relationship is partly explained by a significant negative indirect effect through emotional exhaustion. Moreover, empowering leadership attenuates the positive relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion, and this buffering effect is stronger when POS is high, as indicated by a significant three‐way interaction. These findings contribute to the JD–R literature by providing evidence consistent with the health‐impairment pathway and demonstrating how empowering leadership and POS jointly moderate the relationship between workload and emotional exhaustion.

As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

documents.abstract: Software that allocates tasks, sets the pace of work, monitors behaviour and rates performance has moved from delivery platforms into ordinary workplaces, yet comparative evidence on how widely it is used, who is shielded from it and what it does to job quality remains thin. This study reanalyses the published results of the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) OSH Pulse survey of about 27,250 workers in 29 countries (spring 2022) and sets them against the 2024 establishment survey (ESENER) and the 2025 OSH Pulse wave. A country-by-sector panel of the organisational model index shows that 63 percent of its variation lies between countries and 12 percent between sectors; sector rankings agree across countries (Kendall’s W = 0.28), with commerce, transport and food, ICT and finance, and administrative services highest. Countries with statutory agreement or co-determination rights over new technology do not show lower adoption (difference -0.11 index points; exact permutation p = 0.44). Published regressions link each additional digital management practice to 0.21 more psychosocial risks and 0.17 more health complaints; worker consultation is associated with reductions equal to 0.51 (95% interval 0.32 to 0.70) and 0.78 (0.50 to 1.06) of one practice. Raising consultation to all workers would offset 15 percent of the average psychosocial burden and 22 percent of the health burden, and a package of effective measures 53 and 74 percent. The findings are associations from self-reports, and the panel tests describe variation among cell means rather than sampling error. Purpose - This study measures the diffusion of digital worker management across European countries and sectors, asks whether worker voice institutions are associated with less adoption, and quantifies how far worker consultation offsets the job quality costs of digital management. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published OSH Pulse 2022 results: a two-way variance decomposition and Tukey non-additivity test on a 29-country by 8-sector panel, Kendall’s W, exact permutation and bootstrap comparisons of voice regimes, and delta-method and Monte Carlo accounting built on published regression coefficients. Findings - Country differences dominate sector differences in adoption; sector ranks are stable; voice regimes are not associated with lower adoption; and consultation is associated with sizeable but partial offsets of psychosocial and health burdens. Research limitations/implications - The analysis uses published aggregates and coefficients, cross-sectional self-reports and a coarse regime classification, and cannot establish causal effects or test whether consultation moderates the effect of digital management. Practical implications - Employers and regulators should treat consultation on digital systems as one component of a package that includes information, awareness and transparency, and should extend algorithmic management safeguards beyond platform work. Social implications - Because most workers already experience some form of digital management, protection that applies only to platform workers will miss most of those affected. Originality/value - The paper brings comparative panel evidence, institutional comparison and transparent accounting together, and shows how the current regulatory and survey evidence on digital management fits.

Introduction Supply chain occupations differ in the discretion, coordination, pace, responsibility, and physical activity built into their work. We examined how these conditions correspond to the Work Style requirements associated with occupational performance and whether the resulting profiles distinguish task groups across conventional occupational families. Methods O*NET 30.3 supplied 57 Work Context elements, 21 Work Style Impact ratings, and 41 Work Activity Importance ratings. Principal component analysis (PCA) and permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) compared five families among 24 focal occupations. Elastic Net models were developed from 838 non-focal occupations to predict each Work Style for the 24 focal occupations. Multi-response partial least squares (PLS2) regression evaluated the joint context–style relation across all 862 occupations, and Ward clustering linked occupational profiles to Work Activities. Results Family membership accounted for 35.2% of Work Context variation and 64.5% of Work Style variation. Nine of 21 Work Styles had positive focal-sample R 2 ; self-confidence ( R 2 = 0.589) and stress tolerance ( R 2 = 0.478) were the strongest predictions, whereas empathy was poorly predicted ( R 2 = −2.632). Two clusters separated 19 occupations emphasizing information processing, decision making, and coordination from five emphasizing material handling, equipment operation, and physical work. Their Work Activity profiles differed ( R 2 = 0.314, p = 0.001). Discussion The occupational pattern links decision latitude, consequential responsibility, and coordination demands to particular behavioral requirements, while the task comparison identifies operational similarities that cross family boundaries. Together, the findings support job analysis that combines working conditions, performance-relevant Work Styles, and task content.

AI can automate bounded tasks, augment managerial judgement, or combine both roles across different decision stages. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework explaining how AI adoption influences managerial decision-making and organisational performance through human–AI collaboration and decision implementation. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, sociotechnical systems thinking, decision-making theory, and dynamic capabilities, the paper argues that AI creates value when analytical capabilities complement managerial contextual knowledge and are embedded in accountable routines. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences decision quality through information processing, option generation, and decision support; decision quality contributes to performance when decisions are implemented effectively. documents.abstract: Privately held technology firms valued at more than USD 1 billion (“unicorns”) make high-stakes strategic choices under extreme uncertainty: which markets to enter, when to pivot, how to price, and when to prepare for a public listing. Many have embedded artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into these choices. This paper examines how the depth of AI/ML integration in strategic decision-making is related to decision speed, forecasting accuracy, decision quality, financial performance and strategic agility. Building on bounded rationality, dynamic-capabilities and data-driven-firm theory, we derive five hypotheses and test them on a purpose-built synthetic dataset of 200 global IT unicorns. In the simulated data, a one-standard-deviation increase in AI maturity is associated with 7.4 fewer days in the strategic decision cycle, 2.3 percentage points lower revenue-forecast error and 5.5 points higher decision quality (all p < 0.001). Associations with revenue growth, burn multiple and customer-acquisition payback are conditional on data governance: the interaction terms are statistically significant (p < 0.01), and the positive growth association is concentrated in firms with above-median governance. AI maturity also raises the odds of a successful strategic pivot (odds ratio 1.84) and of IPO readiness (1.79). Sector differences in AI maturity are large (F = 12.1, p < 0.001), whereas regional differences are only marginal (F = 2.1, p = 0.056). Results are stable to robust standard errors, to a rank-based correlation and to splitting the sample by region, but weaker with an alternative maturity proxy. Because the data are synthetic, every relationship reflects the assumptions of the generator. The contribution of the paper is therefore methodological: a transparent measurement framework, hypotheses and estimation strategy that can be re-run on real survey or proprietary data.

documents.abstract: Purpose-driven work has lately become an increasingly important element of employment preferences, particularly among Generation Z. While prior research has primarily examined organisational purpose in relation to meaningful work, work attitudes, and individual characteristics, less is known about how purpose influences employment-related decision-making under trade-off conditions. This study addresses this gap by examining purpose orientation as a decision criterion shaping the acceptance of employment-related trade-offs.The analysis is based on a questionnaire survey conducted among 797 Hungarian higher education students, with a focused subsample of 309 respondents who identified organisational purpose as an important factor in job choice. Using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression, the study investigates whether purpose orientation is associated with MBTI personality characteristics and how it relates to willingness to accept different types of trade-offs.The results indicate that personality-based characteristics provide limited explanatory value for purpose prioritisation in the present sample. By contrast, stronger purpose orientation is associated with a higher likelihood of accepting several employment-related trade-offs, including increased workload, reduced flexibility, lower bonuses, lower job stability, and lower salary. However, financial and security-related compromises remain relatively uncommon overall.These findings suggest that purpose operates as a bounded and context-dependent motivational factor within employment-related decision-making rather than as an unconditional driver of sacrifice. By framing purpose orientation as a criterion within multi-attribute employment decisions, the study contributes to the literature on meaningful work and motivation and provides practical implications for organisations seeking to attract and retain Generation Z employees.

In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

Generative artificial intelligence enables producers to reformulate risky content after moderation, creating feedback between behaviour and governance. We examine how joint weakening across governance stages and differences in response speeds affect risk, trust and local stability. We develop a dimensionless, uncalibrated governance--adaptation evolutionary game linking content producers, platform governance units and users. The model includes finite moderation capacity, provenance retention, trust memory and endogenous producer adaptation. In the tested factorial design, jointly weakening the governance channels increased risk and reduced trust and user-experienced quality; under a common favourable reference, joint deterioration exceeded the corresponding positive single-channel losses for all three outcomes. Along a prescribed composite continuation path, spectral analysis indicated that tenfold acceleration of either backlog or provenance dynamics shifted the estimated local-stability boundary toward stronger aggregate feedback, whereas tenfold acceleration of trust-memory dynamics shifted it toward weaker feedback. These results are conditional on the specified structures and operating states: matching the adaptation state alone did not ensure equivalent transient responses or local stability. The framework supports analysis of governance coordination and response timing; application to particular platforms requires empirical calibration and validation.

documents.abstract: When economic threat is salient, managers focus on preventing losses and neglect the opportunities adaptation requires, a pattern termed threat bias. On the prevailing view, managerial attention is limited so that attention to threat comes at the expense of attention to opportunity: Restoring it means perceiving less threat or relaxing vigilance, and the remedy has been to divide the orientations across people or units. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, in which promotion and prevention are independent systems, I propose instead that threat bias reflects a situational construal: Salient threat makes prevention cues dominant, while promotion cues lie dormant, so their relation is not fixed. I test this with two brief construal-shaping interventions, one highlighting opportunities (opportunity) and one highlighting opportunities and threats (balanced), in a five-wave field experiment with 414 managers during the COVID-19 downturn, with voice rated by higher level managers blind to condition. Among unexposed managers, within-person increases in perceived threat were associated with lower promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, the threat-bias pattern. Both interventions weakened that association and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice relative to control, under sustained economic threat. The balanced intervention also increased prevention focus and threat-related voice; the opportunity intervention changed neither. Mean perceived threat was unchanged: The interventions altered how managers responded to threat, not how much threat they perceived. Intervention effects on voice grew over 3 months. Threat bias therefore reflects how managers construe the situation rather than an unavoidable trade-off between the orientations, and both can be raised in the same managers at once. Este artículo analiza las tensiones estructurales que la opacidad epistémica inherente a los modelos de frontera empleados en agentes inteligentes produce sobre las garantías constitucionales de motivación, trazabilidad y control jurisdiccional. La investigación parte de la constatación de que la autonomía emergente e imposibilidad técnica de reconstruir cadenas causales en la operatividad de estos sistemas hacen inviable el paradigma del control humano significativo, convirtiéndolo en una ficción normativa incapaz de asegurar una responsabilidad efectiva. A partir de este diagnóstico, se adopta un enfoque teórico-dogmático de orientación crítico-analítica para comprender la crisis de legitimidad provocada por la inteligencia artificial generativa. Los resultados muestran que la ausencia de sujetos humanos identificables vinculados causalmente a los efectos de estos modelos genera un vacío estructural de imputación, incompatible con las exigencias del Estado de Derecho. Se concluye que la creación de una personalidad jurídica algorítmica de carácter instrumental, inspirada en antecedentes como el peculium romano, constituye una alternativa normativamente coherente para restablecer centros funcionales de responsabilidad, garantizar la reparación y preservar la coherencia del sistema jurídico en contextos de agencia distribuida.

documents.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

Purpose of Study: This study examined the effect of job rotation procedures on employee engagement at the National Registration Bureau Headquarters in Nairobi City County, Kenya. Specifically, it assessed how job rotation contributes to employee skills development, motivation, teamwork and engagement. The study was guided by the Job Characteristics Model of work design. Methodology: The study adopted a descriptive research design targeting 154 employees through census sampling. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. A total of 146 questionnaires were returned, representing a 94.8% response rate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and regression analysis, alongside qualitative thematic analysis. Findings: The findings revealed positive perceptions of job rotation procedures, particularly skills development (M = 4.24), teamwork (M = 4.22), motivation (M = 4.21) and task exposure (M = 4.17). Employee engagement was high, with mean scores ranging from 4.21 to 4.23. Correlation analysis established a strong positive relationship between job rotation procedures and employee engagement (r = .741, p < .01). Regression analysis demonstrated a statistically significant positive effect (B = 0.312, β = .324, p < .001). These results indicate that structured job rotation procedures are associated with improved employee engagement, supporting the Job Characteristics Model. Conclusion: The study concluded that job rotation procedures significantly enhance employee engagement through skills development, motivation and collaboration. It recommends institutionalising competency-based rotation policies, providing appropriate training, ensuring transparent communication and regularly monitoring implementation. These measures can strengthen employee commitment, promote professional development and improve workforce effectiveness within public institutions.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment, performance evaluation, employee monitoring, and workplace decision-making raises important questions about employee rights, organizational accountability, and the conditions necessary for sustainable work engagement. Although existing research has examined the motivational consequences of AI-enabled work, the integration of employment law, AI governance, and established work-engagement principles remains insufficiently developed. This study develops an integrative analytical framework connecting five established work-engagement principles with AI governance and employment-law considerations in the European context. Drawing on an integrative literature review of motivational theories, contemporary research on AI-enabled work, responsible AI governance, and relevant European Union regulatory instruments, the study examines how five governance dimensions (lawful and proportionate AI use; equality and non-discrimination; employee voice and procedural rights; human oversight and accountability; and transparent evaluation and fair reward allocation) extend the application of these principles to AI-mediated employment. The framework draws on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory to explain how AI-related organizational practices and legal-institutional governance may shape employee experiences and influence whether AI-mediated working conditions are perceived as job resources or job demands, with potential implications for work engagement. The study's originality lies in integrating established AI governance considerations with established work-engagement principles rather than proposing entirely new governance principles. It contributes an interdisciplinary theoretical perspective while recognizing the need for future empirical validation and jurisdiction-specific legal analysis. The framework may inform managerial and policy discussions on developing fair, accountable, and employee-centered AI-enabled workplaces across Europe.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) shape human–AI interaction, yet capability and safety benchmarks provide limited insight into their expressed value priorities. Across three studies, we developed an output-based approach to evaluating correspondence between LLM priorities and human judgements of optimal AI functioning. Study 1 identified six themes through inductive qualitative analysis: Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 found stable rankings within models and a shared priority structure across models. Study 3 compared 75 LLMs with 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric combining profile shape and calibration of between-priority differences. Many models reproduced the human profile while exaggerating differences between priorities. Fidelity varied across models, with no clear pattern linking fidelity to more recent releases. Both humans and LLMs assigned Agency low priority. This framework offers a standardized method for auditing expressed value profiles across models alongside capability, safety, and output evaluations.

documents.abstract: As digital assistants become increasingly integrated into safety-critical environments, explainable AI is expected to support operator understanding and decision-making. From a human-machine interface design perspective, how explanations are presented is an important consideration. This exploratory, design-focused study investigates the usefulness and user experience of storytelling video-based explanations compared with text-based explanations in a simulated emergency involving drone and Urban Air Mobility traffic management. Explanation content was structured using Construal Level Theory to provide incremental levels of detail. Nine licensed air traffic controllers participated in a mixed-methods, within-participants study, assuming the speculative role of UAM Coordinator responsible for low-altitude airspace safety. Eight of nine participants preferred the storytelling video format, describing it as more engaging and supportive of understanding and decision confidence. However, some perceived that the system had already made the decision, raising concerns about human agency. Video also offered limited flexibility for revisiting information, whereas text enabled self-paced reading and review but was perceived as more stressful to process. Rather than establishing the superiority of either format, the findings provide preliminary design insights into balancing engagement, user control, and human agency in explainable AI interfaces for future UAM operations.

Change-oriented behavior (CB), that is, self-directed actions that question and seek to improve how work gets done, is one way employees drive constructive change at work. Although CB is dynamic and primarily driven by affective processes, less is known about individual differences in day-to-day carryover (i.e. the extent to which yesterday’s change behavior predicts today’s) and about the role of inner personal resources, such as emotional appraisal. Integrating cognitive evaluation theory and conservation of resources theory, we examined whether self-emotional appraisal (SEA) and others’ emotional appraisal (OEA) relate to carryover patterns of CB. Employees from Greece (N = 602) completed a quantitative diary over five consecutive workdays. Results from multilevel autoregressive analysis revealed moderate, positive day-to-day CB carryover with significant between-person variation. Both mean levels of SEA and OEA predicted carryover strength, controlling for mean CB and trait affectivity. SEA showed comparable effects on baseline levels and carryover, whereas OEA showed much stronger effects on levels than carryover, suggesting functional differentiation. Baseline CB strongly negatively related to carryover, indicating that behavioral level and temporal carryover represent distinct constructs. The study contributes to both theory and practice by clarifying how distinct emotional competencies support the maintenance of change-directed effort over time.

Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

documents.abstract: This study explores intergenerational vehicle comfort using the Etic-Emic framework, translating a psychological concept into automotive guidelines. A scoping review identified 34 parameters, and trend analysis of 1789 Scopus articles (1953-2025) tracing comfort across vehicle generations. Expert interviews with 15 specialists classified them as Etic (relevant to L0 and L5) or Emic (emerging specifically in L5), suggesting additional factors. Group brainstorming refined classifications, yielding 44 parameters, including factors such as brand identity and cargo space. Safety, vibration control, and fuel efficiency were stable Etic parameters, whereas non-driving tasks, confidence to sleep or fully recline, legal liability transparency, and cybersecurity were Emic. The novel "Intergenerational Car Comfort" concept provides OEMs an actionable decision tool: its Etic-Emic matrix guides trade-offs, including safety constraints versus expectations to recline and sleep. Ultimately, it identifies legacy architectures to retain or those requiring new interior packaging and HMI solutions, providing a roadmap for next-generation automated vehicles.

Generative AI entered universities as a tool that students consult on demand. The next generation of systems, AI agents that plan, remember and act over several steps, will take over parts of teaching, and distance education will feel this first. This article asks how responsibility should be divided between people and such agents in distance higher education. Following design science methodology, it combines an integrative review of experimental and survey evidence published in 2019-2026, regulatory documents and enrolment data for Uzbekistan. The evidence points in one direction: the same models raise or lower learning depending on how they are constrained. An AI tutor built around expert-written scaffolding produced learning gains 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations larger than active learning in class, while unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice scores by 48% but lowered later exam scores by 17%. Student use of AI is close to universal (92-95% in UK surveys, 60-72% in Uzbek samples), yet only about a third of students report receiving institutional training. In Uzbekistan, correspondence and distance students account for 32% of 1.85 million students, with 36 students per teacher. The proposed framework defines five levels of AI agency, from tool to orchestrating agent, and assigns each distance learning task a maximum level using three criteria: the stakes of the decision, the reversibility of errors and the strength of evidence. Tutoring and formative feedback may reach the tutor agent level under teacher oversight, whereas grading, progression and admission remain human decisions. Recommendations for universities and national AI policy follow.

Occupational fatigue poses persistent workforce and safety risks in healthcare. Other safety–critical sectors manage fatigue through structured fatigue risk management systems (FRMS), but whether healthcare’s evidence supports similar system-level claims is unclear. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the effects, implementation, and certainty of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare. PubMed, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 1 June 2026. Studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, synthesized narratively per Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guidance, and assessed for implementation and certainty using Proctor’s framework and GRADE. Thirty-four publications representing 32 studies were included across four strategy groups: work-schedule and duty-hour controls; multicomponent programs and education/coaching; nap and restorative-break practices; and digital monitoring and real-time countermeasures. No included study evaluated a complete, formally governed fatigue risk management system; the evidence concerned isolated or bundled workplace strategies. Naps and restorative breaks showed the most recurrent short-term signals for reduced fatigue/sleepiness and improved vigilance or cognitive performance, though findings were inconsistent; evidence for other strategies was weaker, and patient-safety, organizational, and economic outcomes were rarely evaluated. Implementation evidence concentrated on acceptability and fidelity; organizational governance, structured risk assessment, reach, cost, and sustainability were unexamined, and certainty was predominantly low or very low, with one moderate-certainty exception for increased sleep duration under reduced-duty schedules. Healthcare has thus tested individual countermeasures rather than embedded fatigue risk management within organizational practice; advancing the field requires linking local hazards to supported controls, with particular attention to the governance and risk-assessment structures that remain least developed.
